title: September 22, 1991: India lost the widow who broke a taboo and reshaped who could act on screen.

sources.text: The Quint - Durga Khote: The First Woman, Man Enough to Play a Woman On-Screen

caption:
September 22, 1991: India lost the widow who broke a taboo and reshaped who could act on screen.

Born into a respectable, English-educated family in 1905, she was widowed at 26 with two young sons to raise alone. In 1931 she took a minor role in the silent film Farebi Jaal - a profession her own class considered disreputable for a woman of her background.

She went on to act in roughly 200 films and countless stage productions across five decades, most famously as Jodhabai in Mughal-e-Azam (1960), earning a Filmfare nomination. In 2000, India Today named her among the '100 People Who Shaped India.' In 1983 she received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, Indian cinema's highest honor, for lifetime contribution.

A Viksit Bharat by 2047 needs every field open on merit, not birth or circumstance. Durga Khote didn't wait for acting to become respectable - she walked in out of necessity and made it respectable by being undeniably good at it.
